newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 28.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Monday:
* At the Group of Seven nations meeting in Washington, finance ministers and central bankers hinted they would if necessary intervene in currency markets to stop Japan's trade surplus from expanding.
* Two reports suggest that in the first quarter, the personal computer industry grew by about 16 percent worldwide compared to a year ago.

* A court broadened the plaintiff's powers in a libel case against Time magazine. The suit was filed by a man who helped reveal fake photos about child prostitution in Moscow that the magazine published in 1993.

* After Sports Illustrated published an article containing details of scene from a lesbian party at the Nabisco Dinah Shore LPGA tournament, a large advertiser in the magazine's Golf Plus supplement suspended more than $1 million in ads.
* Compaq plans to introduce a so-called personal computer theatre, which combines a computer with a large-screen television for a price tag of $4,999.
* It remains to be seen if customers and competitors will view the $23 billion merger of Bell Atlantic and NYNEX as a threat to open markets.
* Germany's Kirch Group has invested more than $1 billion into a new digital television service called DF-1, but the service has so far only drawn about 40,000 customers.
* Some of the bigger Web search services are trying to make themselves different from the others.
* Los Angeles remains divided about the progress of efforts to bring new jobs to its inner cities, five years after riots broke out there.
* One airport has been temporarily forced to shut due to a contaminant found in jet fuel and some experts, including those at Boeing worry it could damage aircraft.
* One of the hardest film special effects to pull off is the simulation of lava.
* Cisco Systems has successfully started taking orders on the Internet and is also saving money by handling credit checking, production scheduling, technical support and customer support on-line.
* The Ellie awards, given out by the American Society of Magazine Editors, are desired by editors but barely noticed by the general public.
